summary: Analyzes the events that cause IPv6 enterprise networks to be renumbered and describes current renumbering methods in three categories: during network design, during preparation, and during the renumbering itself. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When an office has to switch to new street numbers, this guide covers why it happens and how to plan, prepare and do the change.

subtitle: How to plan, prepare for, and execute an IPv6 network renumbering in an enterprise.

tldr.problem: Enterprise networks must sometimes change their IPv6 address prefixes due to ISP changes, growth, reorganization, or topology shifts, but renumbering is complex and error-prone.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes renumbering scenarios and describes proven methods in three phases: design decisions that ease future renumbering, preparation steps taken before the event, and operational procedures during the renumbering itself.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can plan and execute renumbering with fewer service disruptions by using DHCP, DNS coordination, gradual transitions, and careful address management.

today: RFC 6879 is an Informational RFC that documents current IPv6 renumbering practices. It has not been obsoleted and remains a primary reference for enterprises planning address space changes.

sections.title: Why Networks Need to Be Renumbered
sections.content:
Enterprise networks sometimes must change their IPv6 address space. This happens when a company switches ISPs (and loses the old ISP's address block), when an ISP reassigns prefixes, when the network is reorganized, or when a company grows, splits, or merges. Unlike switching ISPs by using Provider-Independent addresses, enterprise networks typically use Provider-Assigned addresses, which must change when the provider relationship changes.

This document focuses on IPv6 renumbering in enterprise networks and describes current practices organized into three categories: design choices, preparation, and execution.
sections.eli5: Networks have to change their addresses because ISPs change, companies move, or the network grows, and planners should know how to do it smoothly.

sections.title: When and Why Renumbering Happens
sections.content:
Renumbering is triggered by external factors (such as changing ISPs or receiving new prefixes from an ISP) or internal factors (such as company restructuring, topology changes, or adopting new transition mechanisms). Even within a single ISP, renumbering can occur if the network is moved to a different part of the ISP's topology for performance or service reasons.

Internal renumbering also happens when organizations use Unique Local Addresses (ULAs) alongside Provider-Assigned addresses. This allows internal-only devices to keep their ULA addresses stable while public prefixes change.
sections.eli5: External changes (like a new ISP) or internal changes (like company mergers) can force address changes, and smart design can limit the damage when they happen.

sections.title: Design Decisions That Make Renumbering Easier
sections.content:
Networks designed with renumbering in mind can transition much more smoothly. Key practices include using Fully Qualified Domain Names (FQDNs) instead of embedding IP addresses in configurations; using parameterized configuration that allows addresses to be defined once and reused throughout the network; and delegating prefixes through DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation so addresses flow automatically from routers to hosts.

Operators should also use Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6) or Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC) for all hosts, avoid manual address configuration, and keep DNS records updated automatically. Using Unique Local Addresses for internal-only devices protects them from having to renumber when external prefixes change.
sections.eli5: If you set up your network to use names instead of addresses, and let the system manage addresses instead of hardcoding them, renumbering becomes much easier.

sections.title: Preparing Before Renumbering Occurs
sections.content:
Networks that expect renumbering soon should reduce address and DNS lifetimes before the event. This ensures that hosts and DNS caches do not keep stale addresses for too long. Address preferred lifetimes can be shortened to encourage rapid address changes, while valid lifetimes can remain longer for safety. DNS Time-to-Live (TTL) values on leaf nodes should be reduced so cached records expire quickly. DNS configuration lifetimes on hosts should also be reduced by adjusting the RDNSS option or DHCPv6 lease times.

Organizations should also identify applications with long-lived connections that will need special handling during the transition.
sections.eli5: Before moving, set up your DNS and address configuration to expire quickly so stale information does not hang around and break things.

sections.title: Executing the Renumbering
sections.content:
Renumbering happens over a transition period in which both old and new addresses are in use. Organizations must decide whether to use a flag day (a planned outage) or a gradual transition. Flag days are simpler operationally but cause unavailability, while gradual transitions avoid outages but require more management.

During the transition, DNS records for both old and new addresses should be valid. Hosts receive new addresses through DHCPv6 RECONFIGURE messages or through RA messages with new prefixes. Long-lived application sessions may require session survivability technologies like SHIM6 to continue across address changes. At the end, a thorough verification ensures all devices use only new addresses and that management systems are working correctly.
sections.eli5: During the move, both old and new addresses work for a while, DNS is updated, then old addresses fade away and the new ones take over completely.

sections.title: Security Issues in Renumbering
sections.content:
Automatic renumbering schemes are vulnerable to hijacking by malicious insiders who could forge prefixes to redirect traffic. Securing Neighbor Discovery (SEND) provides cryptographic protection against rogue router advertisements, but deployment is complex. RA-Guard offers a simpler alternative by blocking rogue RA messages at the edge. DHCPv6 has built-in authentication mechanisms, though they are not widely deployed.

Dynamic DNS updates can be exploited for denial-of-service attacks, so update authentication and rate limiting should be used together. Enterprises using frequent ISP changes should consider the routing system risks of overlapping old and new prefixes, though this is rare in normal operation.
sections.eli5: Bad actors could trick the system into sending traffic to the wrong place, so you need security measures to prevent forged address advertisements.
